title: The People You Hire Say More About You Than the People You Promote
author: Lead With Kelly
summary: Hiring decisions reveal more about a leader's character, judgment, and insecurities than any performance review, because hiring is almost entirely the leader's own call—unlike promotions, which are ratified by committees and distributed as shared credit. The author recounts choosing a safe, resume-obvious candidate over a higher-potential candidate she knew was better, only to have the safe candidate decline and the right candidate disappear to another offer. The 'bigger-than-me question'—'Will hiring this person make my team better than I am?'—is identified as the real question every hiring decision must answer, yet the one most leaders unconsciously avoid. Leaders who plateau do so by consistently hiring people who won't challenge or surpass them; leaders who keep growing deliberately hire people who scare them a little, as a discipline not a gesture. Hiring for the role after the current one—not just the immediate opening—builds internal succession pipelines and team reputations as talent factories. A three-question annual talent audit (what do my last five hires say about me, how many have grown beyond their role, and is there at least one person who pushes me?) is offered as a diagnostic for leaders willing to look honestly at the portrait their hires have painted.
points: Hiring is the clearest window into a leader's real standards and insecurities because it is almost entirely their own call, unlike promotions which are distributed across committees.
The 'bigger-than-me question'—will this hire make my team better than I am?—is the only hiring question that actually matters, and the one most leaders unconsciously avoid.
Leaders who plateau hire defensible candidates; leaders who keep growing hire people who scare them a little, as a discipline and not a token gesture.
Hiring for the role after the current one—not just the immediate opening—builds succession pipelines, talent factories, and reputations that compound over time.
quotes: The probability of bad and the probability of right are not the same thing.
Show me who someone hires, and I will tell you where they are still growing. Or where they have stopped.
The leaders who keep growing keep hiring people who scare them a little.
If your last few hires haven't included at least one person whose intelligence, ambition, or capability you weren't fully sure you could keep up with, that's information.
The leaders who build dynasties hire for the role after the one they are filling.
Your promotion list is reviewed by the organization. Your hiring list is reviewed by history.
